title: Particles and density
ks3: Matter: the particle model, changes of state, diffusion, gas pressure and density
intro: Everything is made of tiny particles. Practise solids, liquids and gases, changes of state, diffusion, gas pressure and density.
description: Free KS3 Physics particle model questions with answers: solids, liquids and gases, melting, evaporating and condensing, diffusion, gas pressure and density = mass ÷ volume. Marked instantly, for Year 7, 8 and 9 (ages 9 to 14).

questions.q: In which state are the particles packed closely together in a regular pattern?
questions.hint: Think of ice: it keeps its shape.
questions.explain: In a solid the particles are close together in a regular pattern and can only vibrate on the spot.

questions.q: In which state are the particles far apart and moving fast in all directions?
questions.hint: This state fills any container it is in.
questions.explain: In a gas the particles are far apart and move quickly in all directions, so a gas spreads out to fill its container.

questions.q: Why can a gas be squashed (compressed), but a solid can't?
options: There are big gaps between the gas particles
questions.hint: Compare the spaces between the particles.
questions.explain: Gas particles have big spaces between them, so they can be pushed closer together. Solid particles are already touching.

questions.q: A solid is heated, but it does not melt yet. What happens to its particles?
options: They turn into a different substance
questions.hint: Heating gives the particles more energy.
questions.explain: The particles vibrate more and push a little further apart, so the solid expands slightly. The particles themselves don't get bigger.

questions.q: Which state takes the shape of its container but keeps the same volume?
questions.hint: Think of juice poured from a carton into a glass.
questions.explain: A liquid flows to take the shape of its container, but its volume stays the same. A solid keeps its shape, and a gas spreads out to fill the whole container.

questions.q: Steam and liquid water are both made of water particles. Why does 1 g of steam take up much more space than 1 g of liquid water?
options: The particles in steam are much further apart
The particles in steam are bigger
Steam has more particles in it
The particles in steam weigh less
questions.hint: Compare the spaces between the particles in a gas and in a liquid.
questions.explain: The particles are the same, and 1 g of each has the same number of them. In a gas they are much further apart, so the steam takes up more space and is much less dense.

questions.q: What is it called when a liquid turns into a gas?
questions.hint: Think of a puddle drying up.
questions.explain: A liquid turning into a gas is evaporating. If it happens all through the liquid at its boiling point, it is boiling.

questions.q: What is it called when a gas turns into a liquid?
questions.hint: Think of water drops on a cold window.
questions.explain: A gas turning into a liquid is condensing, like steam forming drops on a cold window.

questions.q: An ice cube with a mass of 20 g melts completely. What is the mass of the water?
questions.hint: The particles are rearranged, but none are added or lost.
questions.explain: Mass is conserved in a change of state: the same particles are still there, so the water has a mass of 20 g.

questions.q: What is it called when a liquid turns into a solid?
questions.hint: Think of putting water in the freezer to make ice cubes.
questions.explain: A liquid turning into a solid is freezing. The opposite, a solid turning into a liquid, is melting.

questions.q: A pan of water is boiling at 100 °C. You keep heating it. What happens to the temperature of the water while it boils?
questions.hint: The energy is being used to change the state.
questions.explain: While the water boils, the temperature stays at 100 °C (at normal air pressure). The energy from the heater is used to pull the particles apart so they escape as a gas, not to make the water hotter.

questions.q: A puddle dries up on a cool day, even though it never gets near 100 °C. Why?
options: Some fast-moving particles at the surface have enough energy to escape into the air
The water soaks up into the clouds straight away
Water can only evaporate when it boils
questions.hint: The particles in a liquid don't all move at the same speed.
questions.explain: This is evaporation. It happens at the surface at any temperature: the fastest particles have enough energy to break away into the air. Bit by bit, the puddle disappears.

questions.q: What is diffusion?
options: Particles spreading out from where there are lots of them to where there are fewer
A liquid turning into a gas
questions.hint: Think of a smell spreading across a room.
questions.explain: In diffusion, particles mix and spread out because they are always moving, from where there are many to where there are fewer.

questions.q: Why does a smell spread more quickly in a warm room than in a cold one?
options: The particles move faster when they are warmer
questions.hint: How does temperature affect how fast particles move?
questions.explain: In a warmer room the particles have more energy and move faster, so they spread out (diffuse) more quickly.

questions.q: A gas is in a sealed box. What causes the gas pressure on the walls?
options: Gas particles sticking to the walls
questions.hint: The particles are always moving.
questions.explain: Moving gas particles keep hitting the walls of the box. Each hit pushes on the wall, and all the pushes together make the pressure.

questions.q: A drop of food colouring is put into a glass of still water and left alone. What happens?
options: The colour slowly spreads through all the water
The colour stays as one drop
The colour sinks and stays at the bottom
The water turns into food colouring
questions.hint: The particles in a liquid are always moving.
questions.explain: The particles of colouring and water keep moving and mixing, so the colour slowly spreads out through all the water. This is diffusion.

questions.q: Under a microscope, tiny specks of smoke in air jiggle about in a random way. What makes them move?
options: Air particles, too small to see, keep hitting them from all sides
The light from the microscope pushes them
questions.hint: The air is made of particles that are always moving.
questions.explain: Air particles are moving fast in all directions and keep bumping into the specks, unevenly from different sides. This random jiggling is called Brownian motion, and it is evidence that particles are moving.

questions.q: In which state does diffusion happen fastest?
options: It is the same in all three
questions.hint: In which state are the particles far apart and moving fastest?
questions.explain: Gas particles move fast and have lots of space between them, so they spread out and mix quickest. Diffusion is slower in liquids and almost does not happen in solids.

questions.q: A block has a mass of 200 g and a volume of 50 cm³. What is its density? (density = mass ÷ volume)
questions.hint: Divide the mass by the volume.
questions.explain: 200 g ÷ 50 cm³ = 4 g/cm³.

questions.q: A metal has a density of 8 g/cm³. What is the mass of 30 cm³ of it?
questions.hint: Mass = density × volume.
questions.explain: 8 g/cm³ × 30 cm³ = 240 g.

questions.q: Water has a density of 1 g/cm³. A block with a density of 0.7 g/cm³ is put in water. What happens?
questions.hint: Compare the two densities.
questions.explain: The block is less dense than water, so it floats.

questions.q: A stone with a mass of 150 g is lowered into a measuring cylinder. The water level rises from 50 cm³ to 80 cm³. What is the density of the stone?
questions.hint: The rise in water level is the volume of the stone.
questions.explain: Volume = 80 − 50 = 30 cm³. Density = 150 g ÷ 30 cm³ = 5 g/cm³.

questions.q: Which is the formula for density?
questions.hint: Density tells you how much mass is packed into each cm³.
questions.explain: Density is the mass in each unit of volume, so density = mass ÷ volume. Its unit can be g/cm³ or kg/m³.

questions.q: Water has a density of 1000 kg/m³. A hot tub holds 1.5 m³ of water. What is the mass of the water?
questions.hint: Mass = density × volume.
questions.explain: Mass = 1000 kg/m³ × 1.5 m³ = 1500 kg. That is as heavy as a car!

questions.q: A wooden block measures 10 cm × 5 cm × 2 cm and has a mass of 60 g. What is its density?
questions.hint: Work out the volume first: length × width × height.
questions.explain: Volume = 10 × 5 × 2 = 100 cm³. Density = 60 g ÷ 100 cm³ = 0.6 g/cm³. That is less than water (1 g/cm³), so it floats.

questions.q: A block of ice has a volume of 100 cm³. Ice has a density of about 0.9 g/cm³ and water has a density of 1 g/cm³. The ice melts. What is the volume of the water?
questions.hint: Find the mass of the ice first. Does the mass change when it melts?
questions.explain: Mass of ice = 0.9 g/cm³ × 100 cm³ = 90 g. Melting does not change the mass, so there is 90 g of water. Volume = 90 g ÷ 1 g/cm³ = 90 cm³. Ice takes up more space than the same water, which is why ice floats.
